title: sherlock: one command asks four hundred sites if you exist

facts.method: repo README, data.json site list and GitHub API numbers, all fetched 2026-11-09
facts.limits: A yes is a username match, not a verified identity; common names collide across sites.

verify_before_render: Every point cites its source in the feature sheet (features.json evidence quotes).
Numbers on screen are the verified ones: 481 sites, 327/127/27 error types, 106,020 stars, GitTrend #1.

scenes.heading: ONE COMMAND FINDS YOU… EVERYWHERE?
scenes.say: How does one command find you on four hundred plus sites at once? It asks them all.

scenes.heading: THE THREE WAYS SITES ANSWER
scenes.say: Three hundred twenty seven answer with a status code. A hundred twenty seven print an error message. Twenty seven just redirect.

scenes.heading: PACKED INTO ONE COMMAND
scenes.say: One open source project packed that trick into a single command. Sherlock.

scenes.heading: TYPE A NAME. IT ASKS.
scenes.say: Type the name, and sherlock fans out the checks, then lists every site that said yes.

scenes.heading: STEADY FOR YEARS. SPIKING TODAY.
scenes.say: And today it is trending number one on GitTrend. One hundred six thousand stars, for a tool from twenty eighteen.

scenes.heading: A NAME MATCH IS NOT A PERSON
scenes.say: But it matches a name, not a person. A common name can say yes for somebody else.

scenes.heading: THE HELP FILE ADMITS IT
scenes.say: Its own help file admits it: ignoring exclusions may return more false positives.

scenes.heading: ASK EVERYONE. HEAR THE NO'S.
scenes.say: So it is not stalking. It is the phone book trick. Ask everyone at once, and listen to how they say no.
Follow for the next repo. Comment sherlock and I will send the link.
